{{< include ../includes/generated-guided-context-en-llm-limits.qmd >}}
::: {.chapter-lead}
Predicting the next token is a **training objective**. What a model gains from it is a matter of evaluation, not definition. This page separates what the objective guarantees — little beyond prediction itself — from what it merely makes plausible.
:::

::: {.callout-note .learning-outcomes collapse="true" title="Learning outcomes"}
By the end of this page, you will be able to:
- distinguish what follows from the training objective from what requires evaluation;
- state the criterion used behind the word "understand";
- explain why an apparent ability depends on the metric and the protocol.
:::

## 1. What the objective guarantees — and does not

A prediction objective learns to assign probabilities to observed token sequences. It can yield linguistic abilities and complex behaviors, but it does not guarantee:

- that every generated statement is true — plausible but false statements, often called *hallucinations*, are the best-known illustration;
- that the probabilities are well calibrated;
- that the model has a human-like understanding of the world;
- that an observed ability generalizes to every task or context;
- that a behavior is causally explained by an isolated attention pattern.

These missing guarantees are not implementation defects: they follow from the objective itself. Each is addressed by an adapted evaluation — metrics, baselines, controls — whose method is the subject of the [Experimental evaluation](experimental-evaluation.qmd) page.

## 2. What does "understand" mean?

The word "understanding" must be made precise. It can denote:

- an **operational competence**, measured on tasks — summarizing, classifying, explaining, or solving a problem;
- a **stronger claim** about human-like understanding, experience, or intention.

Observable performance can support the first interpretation within a given scope; it does not establish the second. State the criterion you use instead of treating "understands" as a single, directly measurable property.

## 3. "Emergent" abilities and scale effects

Discussions of so-called *emergent* abilities require specifying the task, the metric, the thresholds, and the models compared. An ability that seems to appear abruptly under a given metric may depend on measurement resolution or protocol: recent analyses show that several "emergent" effects disappear when the metric is smoothed or replaced. Examine the results, controls, and definitions before concluding a qualitative transition; [experimental evaluation](experimental-evaluation.qmd) makes these requirements explicit. The [debate over emergent abilities](emergence.qmd) examines the protocols and metrics used to test such claims.

Model size alone does not explain performance either. Data quality, diversity, and provenance, the objective, the architecture, the training procedure, adaptation, and the evaluation protocol jointly shape the results.

::: {.callout-tip title="Key ideas in one minute"}
- **Objective:** predicting plausible continuations is not the same as verifying their truth.
- **Calibration:** a high probability is not, by itself, a guarantee of reliability.
- **Understanding:** operational competence measured on a task does not establish human-like understanding.
- **Emergence:** an apparent discontinuity depends on the metric, thresholds, compared models, and protocol.
- **Method:** frame limitations as testable hypotheses and examine them with baselines, controls, and task-appropriate evaluation.

**Quick question:** what observation would distinguish measured improvement from a genuine qualitative transition?
:::

## Primary sources and their role

- [Bommasani et al. (2021), *On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models*](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.07258) — framing of foundation models and their risks.
- The founding papers on emergent capabilities — Wei et al. (2022) and Schaeffer et al. (2023) — and the debate they frame are presented on the [Emergent capabilities](emergence.qmd) page.

Cite the protocol, not just the conclusion.

## Check your understanding

[Exercises and practice](exercises/llm-limits.qmd).

1. A model confidently generates a false statement. Is that necessarily an implementation defect?
2. A capability rises from 0% to 60% on a thresholded metric. What should be examined before claiming emergence?

<details>
<summary>Show the reasoning</summary>

1. No. The prediction objective learns probabilities for observed continuations; it does not guarantee a truth-verification mechanism.
2. Examine the metric, threshold, compared models, and protocol. A thresholded metric can turn gradual improvement into an apparent jump.

</details>
:::
